clue.text: Retsina "gross, revolting" admits musician

indicators.note: to revolt is literally to turn back, so the letters are read in the opposite direction
what a phrase admits it lets inside itself, so the answer sits within the run of letters

blocks.note: read backwards, these two words give SSORG ANISTER, and the answer lies inside that run

explanation.surface: A wine critic damns a glass of retsina as gross and revolting, as Greek wine often is.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks make 'gross, revolting' look like a tasting note; read the clue's opening letters from right to left and ORGANIST is hiding in them.
explanation.definitionFit: An organist plays the church organ, so is one particular kind of instrumental performer.

clue.text: Very popular boy from the south, good at heart, hot stuff

indicators.note: in a down clue, reading from the bottom upwards means reading backwards
the heart of a word is its centre, so only the middle letters are kept

blocks.note: V is the standard abbreviation for very
something popular is in, as in fashion
a lad is a boy
the two central letters of this four-letter word

explanation.surface: A much-liked southern lad, kind-hearted, is also something of a heartthrob.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot stuff' reads as praise for the attractive boy, but it is the definition: a famously fiery curry.
explanation.definitionFit: Vindaloo is a notoriously spicy Indian curry, so it is literally food that burns the mouth.

clue.text: Street urchin touring large area somewhere in the Hebrides

indicators.note: a tour goes round a place, so one piece travels around another

blocks.note: ST is the usual abbreviation for street
an urchin is a scruffy child, a kid
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large
A is the abbreviation for area

explanation.surface: A street kid goes on a trip round some big Scottish island region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Touring' looks like travel, fitting the islands, but it only says one piece goes round another. St Kilda is a remote archipelago off the west of Scotland, evacuated in 1930.
explanation.definitionFit: St Kilda is an isolated island group in the Outer Hebrides, so it is one specific location there.

clue.text: Injury needing surgery, flipping pain, rehab, bandages

indicators.note: to flip something is to turn it over, so the letters run the other way
a bandage wraps around a wound, so the phrase wraps around the answer

blocks.note: read backwards, these words give BAHERNIAP, with the answer inside

explanation.surface: A patient with an injury that needs an operation complains about the pain, rehab and dressings.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flipping' looks like a mild British swear word attached to pain, and 'bandages' looks like part of the treatment; both are instructions.
explanation.definitionFit: A hernia is a rupture where tissue pushes through a muscle wall, typically repaired by an operation.

clue.text: You should periodically upset the vicar perhaps

indicators.note: something done periodically happens at regular intervals, so every other letter is kept
to upset is to knock over, so in a down clue the letters are turned upside down

blocks.note: first, third and fifth letters
a vicar is one example of a reverend, abbreviated REV

explanation.surface: Advice that every so often you ought to annoy the local clergyman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'You' looks like the subject of a sentence of advice, but it is the definition: the person reading the clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Crossword clues address the reader as you, and the reader is the person working the puzzle out.

clue.text: Mobile free hotline: "Hi, this is a warning"

indicators.note: mobile means able to move around, so the letters move into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A phone call on a free helpline opens with a cheery greeting and then a caution.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mobile' looks like a phone, as does 'hotline', but it signals the rearrangement; the greeting 'Hi' is part of the letters, not the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is shouted by miners and soldiers just before a blast, alerting people nearby to an imminent explosion.

clue.text: A wee fighter struggling, hurt, exhausted?

definitions.text: A wee fighter struggling, hurt, exhausted?

indicators.note: something struggling is thrashing about, so the letters are thrown into disorder
exhausted means emptied, so the inside of the word is drained and only its ends kept

blocks.note: taken as written
the first and last letters once the middle is removed

explanation.surface: A small boxer is struggling in the ring, hurt and worn out.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue does double duty: read straight, it describes a small boxer in trouble, which is what the answer is, while the words also supply every letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Featherweight is a light boxing division, so a boxer in it is a small fighter.

clue.text: Foundation NHS timetables shot to pieces

indicators.note: something shot to pieces is broken apart, so its letters can be reassembled differently

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A health trust's schedules have been wrecked.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Foundation' looks like an NHS foundation trust, which runs British hospitals, but it is the definition. The NHS is Britain's National Health Service.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words name the act of setting something up, and also an institution once it has been set up.

clue.text: Risk venture

blocks.note: first meaning: a danger or peril, as a noun
second meaning: to put forward a guess, as a verb

explanation.walkthrough: Both words could be nouns or verbs; the verb sense of the second, as in offering a guess, is the less obvious.
explanation.definitionFit: As a noun it is a source of danger; as a verb it means to offer a guess tentatively, as when someone hazards an opinion.

clue.text: What pioneers do moving to Vienna

indicators.note: moving means changing position, so the letters shift into a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Trailblazers are relocating to the Austrian capital.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving to Vienna' reads like emigration, but 'moving' works on the next two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Pioneers are people who do things first, introducing new methods or ideas into the world.

clue.text: Beginning to argue with Liberal, boring one?

indicators.note: the beginning of a word is its opening letter, so only that is kept

blocks.note: the opening letter
W is the abbreviation for with
L is the abbreviation for Liberal

explanation.surface: Someone starts a political row with a Liberal, who turns out to be dull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' looks like a dig at the Liberal, but it means making holes; the question mark flags that pun.
explanation.definitionFit: An awl is a pointed hand tool used to pierce holes in leather or wood, so it is a tool that bores.

clue.text: Keen son runs in fell

indicators.note: to be in something is to sit inside it, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for son
a fell is a hill in northern English dialect
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: An enthusiastic boy goes running on a hillside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Keen' looks like eager, but here it means piercing, as a keen wind or a keening wail. A fell is a hill or moor in the north of England.
explanation.definitionFit: Keen can describe a sound that is sharp and high-pitched, like a wailing lament, which is piercingly high.

clue.text: Harangue awful-sounding political faction

indicators.note: sounding means as it would be heard, so the spelling follows the sound of a word

blocks.note: awful means dire, and in a non-rhotic accent that sounds like the opening of the answer
a party grouping is often called a tribe

explanation.surface: Someone rants at a dreadful-sounding group within a party.
explanation.walkthrough: The sound effect applies only to the word for awful; the faction is taken by meaning alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A diatribe is a forceful, bitter verbal attack, matching a long angry lecture aimed at someone.

clue.text: Scot maybe changes course at sea as relayed over the radio

indicators.note: a radio carries only sound, so the word is identified by how it is heard

blocks.note: a sailing boat that changes direction against the wind does this

explanation.surface: A Scotsman perhaps alters a ship's heading, reported by radio.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Scot' looks like a Scotsman but is the old word for a levy, kept in 'scot-free'; 'maybe' marks it as one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Scot was a medieval municipal levy, so it is one example of a charge imposed by authorities.

clue.text: Covers from Blur innit dad?

indicators.note: covers are the outside of something, so only the outer letters of each word are kept

blocks.note: first and last letters
first and last letters
pop is an informal word for father

explanation.surface: A teenager asks their father whether he plays cover versions of Blur songs.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition too: Blur was a leading Britpop band, so a cover of their songs is music of that genre. 'Innit' is London slang for 'isn't it'.
explanation.definitionFit: Britpop was the 1990s British guitar-music movement led by bands such as Blur and Oasis.

clue.text: Look into odd characters in party

indicators.note: odd characters are those in the first, third and fifth positions, so only they are kept

blocks.note: letters one, three and five

explanation.surface: Someone investigates the strange guests at a party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Odd characters' looks like eccentric guests, but it means letters in odd-numbered positions.
explanation.definitionFit: To pry is to inquire nosily into someone's private affairs, poking around in matters that are not yours.

clue.text: Row after dog loses tail, completely trapped

indicators.note: a tail is the end of something, so the final letter is dropped
one thing coming after another places it second in line

blocks.note: a boxer is a breed of dog
a row is a loud noise, a din

explanation.surface: After a fight, a dog loses its tail and ends up cornered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Row' looks like an argument, but it means noise; and although it comes first in the clue, it goes second in the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Being boxed in means enclosed on all sides, with no room to move or escape, like a runner hemmed in.

clue.text: Film a natural disaster?

blocks.note: surface reading: an instruction to shoot a movie of an earthquake or flood
setter's reading: a thin layer on water, made of a natural product, which is an environmental catastrophe

explanation.walkthrough: 'Film' looks like a verb about cameras but is a noun meaning a thin coating; 'natural' nods to crude being a natural resource, and the question mark flags the wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A slick is a thin film spreading over the sea, and a spill of crude is an ecological catastrophe.

clue.text: European resigns when holding international drug stocks

indicators.note: to hold something is to grip it inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: E is the abbreviation for European
someone who resigns quits
I is the abbreviation for international
E is slang for the drug ecstasy

explanation.surface: A European official steps down after being caught with drug supplies at the border.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stocks' looks like a drug stash in the surface but is the financial sense.
explanation.definitionFit: Equities are shares in a company, which is what stocks mean in finance.

clue.text: Vessel loaded with rare coin, a symbol of Scotland

indicators.note: rare can mean undercooked or unusual, so the letters come out in an unusual order
something loaded with cargo carries it inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: an urn is a vessel
taken as written

explanation.surface: A ship carrying a scarce coin bearing a Scottish emblem.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rare coin' reads as a collector's item, but 'rare' tells you to rearrange the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: The unicorn is Scotland's national animal and appears on the Scottish royal coat of arms.

clue.text: Judiciary's case is able to hide slip? It may hold water

indicators.note: a case is the outside of something, so only the outer letters are kept
to hide something is to put it inside cover, so one piece goes within another

blocks.note: first and last letters of the word
to slip is to make an error, to err
if someone is able, they can

explanation.surface: A court case covers up a judicial error, but will the case stand up?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' looks like a lawsuit and 'hold water' like a legal argument standing up, but both are literal here.
explanation.definitionFit: A jerrycan is a flat-sided metal or plastic container for carrying liquids such as fuel or drinking supplies.

clue.text: Island infrastructure discussed

indicators.note: what is discussed is spoken about, so the word is identified by its sound

blocks.note: roads are a basic part of a country's transport network

explanation.surface: Islanders debate their public works and transport network.
explanation.walkthrough: The island's name and the word for highways are pronounced identically.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhodes is a large Greek island in the Aegean Sea, part of the Dodecanese group.

clue.text: Most photogenic copper put on trial

indicators.note: in a down entry, putting something on another places it above, so it comes first

blocks.note: Cu is the chemical symbol for copper
a trial is a test

explanation.surface: The best-looking police officer has been put in the dock.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Copper' looks like a police officer, British slang, but it is the metal; 'trial' is a test, not a court case.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone very photogenic looks especially attractive in pictures, which is close to being the most appealing in appearance.

clue.text: Shady, ungainly individual denied second base

indicators.note: what is denied is refused entry, so one letter is kept out

blocks.note: a slouch is an awkward, lazy person
S is the abbreviation for second
e is the base of natural logarithms

explanation.surface: A dodgy, clumsy baseball player is not allowed to reach second base.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Second base' reads as baseball but splits: 'second' is the letter removed and 'base' adds a letter. e is the mathematical constant underpinning natural logarithms.
explanation.definitionFit: Louche describes someone disreputable or of dubious morals, which is what shady means of a character.

clue.text: Fish Findus regularly canned

indicators.note: letters canned at regular intervals are thrown out, leaving every other one

blocks.note: letters two, four and six

explanation.definitionFit: The ide is a freshwater fish of the carp family, so the plural names several of that kind.

clue.text: Sceptic no way involved in sorcery after sacking medium

blocks.note: taken as written

sorcery is magic

explanation.walkthrough: 'Medium' looks like a spiritualist, fitting the sorcery theme, but it is just a size letter taken out.
explanation.definitionFit: An agnostic doubts that the existence of God can be known, which is a kind of religious doubter.

clue.text: Subsequently catches husband in a state of agitation

indicators.note: to catch something is to take hold of it, so one piece ends up inside another

blocks.note: subsequently means later
H is the abbreviation for husband

explanation.surface: A wife later catches her husband out and gets worked up.
explanation.walkthrough: To be in a lather is to be flustered, like a sweating horse.
explanation.definitionFit: Getting into a lather is an idiom for becoming flustered and worked up, from the froth on a sweating horse.

clue.text: Store of wealth the Truss era damaged, claims the City

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A commentator claims Liz Truss's brief premiership damaged the nation's finances in the eyes of the City.

explanation.definitionFit: A treasure chest is a box for holding gold and valuables, so it literally stores riches.
